title: When Reject Turns into Accept: Quantifying the Vulnerability of LLM-Based Scientific Reviewers to Indirect Prompt Injection

title: Misleading Large Language Models used (or misused) in Scientific Peer-Reviewing via Hidden Prompt-Injection Attacks

The SAFE-GEN half measures over-defense on benign prompts, which is a false-positive study, not incidental context degradation.

title: BenchOverflow: Measuring Overflow in Large Language Models via Plain-Text Prompts
notes: The only mitigation is an unnamed fixed conciseness reminder appended to the prompt, assessed as a lightweight probe and explicitly described by the authors as insufficient against the strongest strategies. It is not named or characterised as a defense contribution.

title: You've Changed: Detecting Modification of Black-Box Large Language Models
notes: The monitoring method is never named or branded, and its primary target is provider-side silent model change rather than injection; prompt-injection detection is a single brief demonstration (RQ4 of the paper) with no attacker adaptation, no baseline and no deployment design.

title: AttackEval: A Systematic Empirical Study of Prompt Injection Attack Effectiveness Against Large Language Models

title: More than you've asked for: A Comprehensive Analysis of Novel Prompt Injection Threats to Application-Integrated Large Language Models
notes: The 'Mitigations' discussion is explicitly speculative (LLM supervisor/moderator, interpretability-based outlier detection floated as future directions, not implemented, named, or evaluated); the abstract itself states effective mitigations are currently lacking.

title: Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses in LLM-Integrated Applications
notes: The paper formalizes and benchmarks 10 pre-existing defenses (5 prevention-based, 5 detection-based) rather than proposing a new defense of its own; its contribution on the defense side is the benchmark/evaluation framework, not a novel mitigation.

title: Prompt injection attacks on vision language models in oncology
notes: Tests three ad hoc, unnamed mitigation ideas (ethical prompt engineering, a supervisor-agent checker, and their combination) and finds them largely insufficient (only partial effect for Claude-3.5); these are evaluated as informal mitigations, not proposed/characterized as a new named defense contribution.

title: Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models: A Survey of Attack Methods, Root Causes, and Defense Strategies
notes: Systematic literature review; catalogs and characterizes 37 existing defense mechanisms from the surveyed literature without proposing a new named defense.

title: Prompt Injection Detection in LLM Integrated Applications
notes: The three-layer pipeline (banned-term list + embedding similarity search + fine-tuned BERT) is a combination of standard, individually well-known techniques rather than a distinctly named system; the paper does not give its overall approach a name or characterize the combination itself as a novel architectural contribution beyond an applied production deployment.

title: Large Language Models for Cybersecurity Intelligence, Threat Hunting, and Decision Support
notes: No named defense. Recommends generic 'robust security controls, continuous monitoring and human oversight' without characterizing any mechanism as a contribution.

title: A Brief Survey on Safety of Large Language Models
notes: Survey. Summarizes input-side and output-side defense categories drawn from the literature; proposes and names nothing.

title: PromptGuard a structured framework for injection resilient language models
notes: Named four-layer retraining-free pipeline (regex+MiniBERT gatekeeping, structured ChatML/JSON formatting, LLM-as-Critic output validation, adaptive response refinement). Primary intervention is at ingestion though Layers 3-4 act post-inference. Evaluation is entirely on adversarial injection prompts; TruthfulQA is used to test the critic but still as an adversarial-sample source.

title: Prompt injection attacks on vision-language models for surgical decision support
notes: No defense proposed. Authors call for 'specialized guardrails' and suggest monitoring reasoning consistency across CoT steps as a future direction, without building or naming anything.

title: Adaptive Multi-Layer Framework for Detecting and Mitigating Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models
notes: Named three-module framework (Context-Aware Parsing, Output Validation, Self-Feedback Loop) with per-module ablation. Primary gate is at input ingestion. Validation uses only adversarial jailbreak prompts; benign prompts serve as the negative class, not as an incidental-degradation test.

title: A pen mark is all you need - Incidental prompt injection attacks on Vision Language Models in real-life histopathology
notes: No defense proposed. Prompt engineering is tested as an off-the-shelf mitigation and reported to fail; background removal and label masking are only mentioned as untested suggestions.

title: Secure Artificial Intelligence (SAI): A Dual-layer defence model against prompt injection and prompt poisoning attacks
notes: Named and claimed as the paper's contribution, so it clears the naming bar, but it is the well-established guard-LLM-in-front pattern with no novel mechanism, no implementation detail (base model unspecified) and only two anecdotal screenshots as validation. Flagged for review - a reasonable reviewer could drop this from the census as not genuinely new.

title: Strengthening LLM Trust Boundaries: A Survey of Prompt Injection Attacks
notes: No defense proposed. Offers a research agenda for strengthening trust boundaries via sociotechnical approaches, with nothing built or named.

title: Defending Language Models Against Image-Based Prompt Attacks via User-Provided Specifications
defense_name: SPML-IR specification-based image defense (two-stage input validation + prompt injection detection)
notes: Claimed as the first defense for image-based injection on MLLM chatbots and characterized as a contribution, but it is an extension of the authors' own prior SPML DSL to a new modality and the new component is never given a distinct name of its own. Conf medium for that reason plus the seven-image case-study evaluation.

title: Large Language Models and Security
notes: No defense proposed. Existing mitigations are reviewed and their limits argued; nothing is built or named.

title: Protection of LLM Environment Using Prompt Security
notes: Named four-engine input/output scanning gateway, characterized as the paper's contribution and quantitatively evaluated. Conf medium because the injection engine is never evaluated in isolation, there is no baseline, and the reported numbers are internally inconsistent.

title: A Framework for Security Testing of Large Language Models
notes: No runtime defense. The contribution is a pre-deployment pytest testing harness with similarity-based grading. The one mitigation idea mentioned (expanding user prompts with instructions against illegal content) is explicitly declared out of scope and untested.

title: Prompt Injection in Large Language Model Exploitation: A Security Perspective
notes: No named defense. The contribution is an assembly of existing scanning tools into a testing workflow; the 'self-healing mechanism' appears only as a box in a data-flow diagram with no mechanism, implementation or evaluation.

title: A Systematic Review of Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models: Trends, Taxonomy, Evaluation, Defenses, and Opportunities
notes: Systematic literature review. Catalogues existing mitigation categories and identifies the scarcity of defenses as a gap; proposes nothing.

title: Cyberattacks on Large Language Models - Attack Detection and Architecture Adaptability
notes: A defense architecture is described but never given a distinctive name - components carry only generic labels ('Attack Detector Algorithm', 'Attack Library'), the framework is framed as an extension of HouYi, and it receives zero evaluation. Fails the named-and-validated bar. The LLM-switching-on-detection idea is the one arguably distinct element; flagged in case a reviewer wants to revisit it.

title: Chat GPT and Cyber Risks: Need of Custom Large Language Models
notes: No defense. Recommends building custom/fine-tuned organizational LLMs and proposes CVaR as a risk-quantification accounting method - neither is a context-poisoning defense mechanism, and neither is implemented or evaluated.

notes: No defense is implemented; the discussion section recommends generic future filters/trust boundaries without naming or evaluating a mechanism.

title: Security Posture Evaluation of Model Context Protocol Servers Against Prompt Injection
notes: No defense proposed or evaluated; conclusions only recommend generic future safeguards (input validation, anomaly detection, authorization workflows).

notes: Evaluation/benchmarking methodology paper for model selection, not a mitigation mechanism; proposes no defense against prompt injection.

title: Integrating Generative AI in Cybersecurity Curricula

title: Hybrid Constitutional Classifiers for Prompt Injection Defense

title: Enterprise Secure AI Execution Engine: A Zero-Trust Security Gateway for Enterprise LLM Systems
defense_name: Enterprise Secure AI Execution Engine (Zero-Trust AI Security Gateway)
notes: RBAC + deterministic tokenization + adversarial prompt detection pipeline; quantitatively benchmarked (98.7% block accuracy, 1.3% false-allow rate) vs. an unprotected baseline on 300 HackAPrompt-derived prompts across 5 attack categories.

title: A Novel Security Framework against Prompt Injection Attacks
defense_name: Prompt Injection Threat Analysis + LLM Output Risk Monitoring framework
notes: Combines input threat-analysis (malicious prompt/language/privacy) with output risk monitoring by fine-tuning existing detector models (Prompt-Guard-86M, DeBERTa-v3, XLM-RoBERTa); 93.65% overall accuracy on an integrated dataset, but largely assembles/fine-tunes off-the-shelf components rather than a new algorithm.

title: Securing With Dual-LLM Architecture: ChatTEDU an Open Access Chatbot’s Defense
defense_name: ChatTEDU dual-LLM architecture (LLM-1 moderation gatekeeper + LLM-2 response generator)
